planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Carlson 3 is among the most cold-hardy northern pecans available.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Carlson 3 is an ultra-northern pecan selected by I.N. Carlson in Mercer County, Illinois and tested at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, extending reliable pecan cropping far north of the usual commercial range. It produces a small, early-ripening oblong nut (roughly 111 nuts per pound) with golden-brown kernels, trading nut size for the ability to mature a crop in a short northern growing season. It remains a valuable choice alongside other far-northern selections like Colby and Witte for home orchardists above the usual pecan belt.
sources: University of Nebraska-Lincoln nut tree trials

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Lucas needs a protandrous partner since it is itself protandrous.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Lucas is a native seedling pecan found near Goshen, Ohio and now propagated by Grimo Nut Nursery and Nolin River Nut Tree Nursery for its remarkable cold hardiness, surviving temperatures down to roughly -20°F. It also shows outstanding natural scab resistance, recording zero lesions in field trials alongside the well-regarded 'Warren 346' cultivar. Its medium-size nut and protandrous flowering habit make it a strong choice for a northern home orchard wanting a disease-tolerant, winter-hardy pecan.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grainger is a viable pollinizer as well as a strong nut producer.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Grainger was discovered in Tennessee in 1935 and is often cited as the best shagbark hickory selection available, with a nut approaching the size of a shellbark hickory's. It is productive and healthy, serves as a viable pollinizer for other shagbark selections, and ripens late-mid to late October. As with all hickories, expect a long juvenile period before a grafted tree bears its first crop, and plant deep, fertile soil to support the long taproot this species develops.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Neilson is pollen-sterile and needs another shagbark hickory nearby to fruit.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Neilson was selected near Waterford, Ontario for its large, well-filled nut with very good cracking qualities. It is hardy and annually productive with early-ripening nuts, but is pollen-sterile, so a second shagbark hickory cultivar must be planted nearby to ensure fruit set. Give it deep, undisturbed soil to support the long taproot typical of this species and be prepared for a decade or more before a grafted tree reaches full bearing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Fox is well suited to New England and other northern climates.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Fox is a New York-origin shagbark hickory selection well adapted to New England and other cold northern climates where fewer named selections thrive reliably. Its nut is not the largest among shagbark cultivars, but it shells easily and carries very good flavor, making it a practical choice for a northern home nut orchard prioritizing hardiness and ease of cracking over sheer nut size. Expect the typical long juvenile period before a grafted tree begins bearing.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; shellbark hickory develops a long taproot and resents transplanting once established.

directions: Plant in deep, moist, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Fayette produces a very large, walnut-sized nut that is well-filled and ripens annually, maturing mid-to-late October. Like other shellbark hickories it performs best in rich, consistently moist soil similar to its native bottomland habitat, and develops a long taproot that makes it best planted while young rather than transplanted later. It complements other named shellbark selections like Henry and Keystone in a nut-orchard planting focused on this larger-fruited hickory species.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hansen is self-fruitful and bears at a relatively young age for a Persian walnut.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hansen is a Carpathian-strain Persian walnut first recorded in 1934 and remains among the hardiest named Persian walnut cultivars available, surviving temperatures down to roughly -31°C. It bears a small-to-medium, thin-shelled nut with about 60% kernel, is self-fruitful so a single tree can produce a crop, and shows good resistance to blight and anthracnose. Its smaller mature stature of around 30 feet also makes it more manageable for a home orchard than many full-size walnut cultivars.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Ames is protandrous and benefits from a protogynous partner.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Ames emerged from Iowa State University cold-hardy walnut trials and is valued for its productivity, hardiness, and drought tolerance alongside good blight resistance. It ripens mid-season and produces large, oval, easy-cracking nuts, making it a practical choice for a Midwestern home nut orchard. Being protandrous, it sets the heaviest crops when paired with a protogynous Persian walnut cultivar for overlapping bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; North Platte is protandrous and benefits from a protogynous partner.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; North Platte was selected in Nebraska and carries the cold hardiness of its zone 5a origin, producing large, oval, easy-cracking nuts with good resistance to blight. Being protandrous, it sets the heaviest crops when paired with a protogynous Persian walnut cultivar for overlapping bloom timing. It extends the recommended Persian walnut range further north than many commercial cultivars can reliably survive.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees (grafted stock establishes faster than seedling) in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mitchell can occasionally abort part of a heavy midsummer crop, which is normal for this hybrid.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mitchell is by far the most widely propagated named buartnut, a natural butternut-heartnut hybrid found as a parent tree in Scotland, Ontario. It produces a heartnut-shaped nut with cracking qualities superior to plain butternut, combined with hardiness approaching butternut and resistance to butternut canker, a serious disease that has devastated wild butternut populations. It is a very heavy producer that occasionally aborts part of its midsummer crop under heat or moisture stress, which growers should expect as normal rather than a sign of a problem.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Craxezy is named for its unusually easy nut-cracking quality, a genuine advantage for home processing.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Craxezy is a Michigan-origin butternut selection valued for high yield, early leafing, and medium-size nuts that crack unusually well, which is the source of its name and a real practical advantage over the notoriously stubborn shells of most butternuts. It shows some resistance to walnut leaf blotch, a useful trait given how disease-pressured wild butternut populations have become from butternut canker. As with other butternuts, expect an irregular, alternating bearing pattern from year to year.
sources: USDA Forest Service nut tree literature

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Harvest King is a female selection, so a male ginkgo must be nearby for nut production, and the fallen fruit has a notably strong odor worth siting away from walkways.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a male ginkgo for pollination; Harvest King is a female Chinese selection chosen specifically for nut quality rather than fall foliage color, and is the earliest-ripening nut-producing ginkgo, with nuts dropping mid-to-late October. Grafted trees begin bearing at around 10 years of age, far sooner than seedling ginkgoes, which can take decades. Collect the fallen fruit promptly, since the fleshy outer coating has a strong, unpleasant odor as it decomposes, and process the inner nut (the edible part) separately for roasting.

planting.note: Plant container trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; King of Dong Ting is a female selection, so a male ginkgo must be nearby for nut production.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun alongside a male ginkgo for pollination; King of Dong Ting is a female Chinese cultivar selected specifically for nut flavor, producing a large oval fruit and nut prized in Chinese culinary tradition. Grafted trees typically begin bearing between 6 and 10 years of age, considerably sooner than seedling-grown ginkgoes. Collect the fallen fruit promptly once it drops, since the fleshy outer coating has a strong odor as it decomposes, and process the inner nut separately for roasting or traditional Chinese dishes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Titan blooms later than most almonds, dodging spring frost that damages earlier-blooming cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Titan is a notably cold-hardy almond that can be grown well north of the commercial almond range typical of California's Central Valley, thanks to its late bloom time that helps it dodge damaging spring frosts. It produces a thin, well-sealed shell with a high-quality sweet kernel, making it a practical home-orchard choice for gardeners outside the usual almond belt who still want reliable nut production. Give it the same well-drained, sunny site other stone fruits need, and expect it to need a compatible almond or peach pollinator for best fruit set.
